blocks.text: Kinetic theory, extended to astrophysical systems such as stars and galaxies, helps us understand how stars evolve. Stellar evolution is the way a star changes over time. Stars have lifetimes ranging from a few million to trillions of years, and the life of a star depends on its mass.

blocks.title: Which stars live longest
blocks.text: The book says 'the most massive have longer life'. It is the other way round: massive stars burn their fuel very quickly and live only a few million years, while the least massive stars (red dwarfs) live for trillions of years, longer than the present age of the universe. The book itself says this about red dwarfs later in the section.

All stars form from clouds of gas and dust called nebulae or molecular clouds. As such a cloud contracts under gravity, its density and temperature rise, because the kinetic energy of its particles increases (K.E. is proportional to T); the contracting cloud is a proto-star. After millions of years a proto-star can become a star in a state of equilibrium. Figure 13.4 shows the competition between gravity and pressure: as the temperature rises, the internal pressure rises too, and a stable star forms when the inward gravitational force is exactly balanced by the outward pressure. This is described by the hydrostatic equation dP/dr = -G Mr rho_r / r^2, where P is the pressure inside the star, dP/dr the rate of change of pressure with distance r from the centre, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2, Mr the mass enclosed within radius r and rho_r the density at radius r. The negative sign shows that pressure decreases outward while gravity pulls inward.

blocks.alt: Three panels, each a star drawn as a yellow circle with red arrows pointing inward (gravity) and blue arrows pointing outward (gas pressure). Balanced: equal arrows, a stable star. Gravity greater than pressure: thicker red arrows, the star contracts and heats up. Pressure greater than gravity: thicker blue arrows, the star expands, for example into a red giant. Below: the hydrostatic equilibrium equation dP/dr = -G Mr rho_r / r^2.
blocks.caption: Gravity against gas pressure in a star (original diagram after Figure 13.4).
blocks.long_description: A star is a ball of hot gas held together by its own gravity. It stays the same size only while the outward pressure of its hot gas exactly balances gravity; if either wins, the star contracts or expands.

blocks.text: If the balance is not maintained there are two possibilities: if gravity is greater than the internal pressure the star contracts and heats up; if the internal pressure is greater the star expands. As the core temperature rises, nuclear fusion begins: hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium, releasing an immense amount of energy that powers the star for most of its life and holds it against gravitational collapse.

With further rises in temperature and changes in the core, the star may expand to become a red giant. Stars of at least about half the Sun's mass can then fuse helium into heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen, and in more massive stars fusion continues in stages up to iron. The final fate of a star depends mainly on its mass. When a star has used up its fuel it can no longer support itself against gravity. In low- and intermediate-mass stars the core contracts into a dense white dwarf and the outer layers are thrown off as a planetary nebula. Stars of roughly ten times the Sun's mass or more end in a supernova explosion, in which the iron core collapses to form a neutron star or a black hole. Red dwarfs, with their low mass and slow use of fuel, evolve so slowly that the universe is not yet old enough for any red dwarf to have completed its life; models suggest they will slowly become hotter and brighter before ending as low-mass white dwarfs.

blocks.alt: A flow chart. A stellar nebula of gas and dust leads to two paths. Top: an average star like the Sun becomes a red giant, then a planetary nebula, then a white dwarf. Bottom: a massive star becomes a red supergiant, then a supernova, then a neutron star or a black hole. A note says the final fate depends mainly on mass.
blocks.caption: Life cycle of a star (original diagram after Fig 13.5).
blocks.long_description: Both paths start the same way, but a massive star's gravity is strong enough to collapse its core violently. The book's figure labels the explosion stage 'Positron'; it is a supernova.

blocks.text: Neutron stars are among the densest known objects, second only to black holes. Because of their extremely high density, the matter inside behaves like a degenerate gas, and their strong gravity makes them hard to model. By NASA's estimates there may be up to a billion neutron stars in the Milky Way. Many of those observed are young and rotate rapidly, sending out beams of radiation; these are pulsars. Pulsar radiation is thought to be produced when strong magnetic fields channel matter towards the magnetic poles. When a star collapses to form a neutron star its magnetic field is greatly strengthened, because the field lines are squeezed closer together.

blocks.alt: Left: a circular section of a neutron star with a thin outer atmosphere ring and a core of neutrons; blue arrows point outward (neutron degeneracy pressure) and red arrows point inward (gravity). Right: facts from the text: among the densest objects, second only to black holes; a teaspoon of its matter has a mass over 5.5 x 10^12 kg; the whole Earth at this density would fit in a sphere about 305 m across; pulsars are young, fast-spinning neutron stars sending beams from their magnetic poles.
blocks.caption: A neutron star (original diagram after Fig 13.6).
blocks.long_description: In a neutron star, ordinary gas pressure can no longer resist gravity; the pressure that holds it up comes from neutrons packed so tightly that they resist being squeezed further.

blocks.title: For your information
blocks.text: A neutron star is so dense that one teaspoon of its material would have a mass over 5.5 x 10^12 kg, about 900 times the mass of the Great Pyramid of Giza. The whole mass of the Earth at neutron-star density would fit into a sphere 305 m in diameter.

The Sun is the nearest star to Earth and the main source of heat and light for our planet. It formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a huge cloud of gas and dust called the solar nebula. Gravitational contraction raised the temperature at the centre and a protostar formed; when the core became extremely hot, nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium began, releasing a large amount of energy. The life stages of the Sun are nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, planetary nebula and white dwarf. At present the Sun is in its main-sequence stage, producing heat and light by converting hydrogen into helium; it transfers this energy mainly by radiation.

blocks.alt: A timeline from birth to 14 billion years. Yellow circles, slowly growing, show the Sun on the main sequence from birth to about 9 billion years, with an arrow marking now at about 4.6 billion years and the label gradual warming. A large red circle near 10 billion years is the red giant, a dashed circle near 11 is the planetary nebula, and small grey dots from 12 to 14 are the white dwarf. Sizes are not to scale.
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the Sun (original timeline after the book's figure, also numbered Fig 13.5).
blocks.long_description: The Sun is roughly halfway through its main-sequence life. It will slowly warm, swell into a red giant, throw off its outer layers and end as a white dwarf; it is not massive enough to become a supernova.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: A parsec is a unit of distance used by astronomers as an alternative to the light-year, just as kilometres are used as an alternative to miles. One parsec is about 3.26 light-years, or almost 19 trillion miles (31 trillion km).
Worked examples: is a star stable?

The book compares a rough estimate of the gravitational pressure, Pg about G M^2 / R^4, with the star's internal pressure. Example 13.5: a star has mass 1 x 10^30 kg, radius 1 x 10^9 m and internal pressure 5 x 10^14 Pa. Pg = (6.67 x 10^-11)(1 x 10^30)^2 / (1 x 10^9)^4 = 6.67 x 10^49 / 10^36, about 6.67 x 10^13 Pa. The internal pressure is larger, so the star will expand and may evolve into a red giant. Example 13.4: a massive star has mass 4 x 10^30 kg, radius 5 x 10^8 m and internal pressure 1 x 10^14 Pa. Pg = (6.67 x 10^-11)(4 x 10^30)^2 / (5 x 10^8)^4 = 1.07 x 10^51 / 6.25 x 10^34, about 1.7 x 10^16 Pa. Gravity is stronger, so the star will contract and may eventually collapse, possibly forming a neutron star or a black hole.

blocks.title: Check the arithmetic in Examples 13.3 and 13.4
blocks.text: Example 13.3 (mass 2 x 10^30 kg, radius 7 x 10^8 m, internal pressure 1.0 x 10^14 Pa) prints Pg = 2.668 x 10^50 / 2.401 x 10^35 as about 1.3 x 10^14 Pa and calls the star stable. The division gives about 1.1 x 10^15 Pa, roughly ten times the internal pressure, so on these figures gravity would win. Example 13.4 prints 1.7 x 10^15 Pa; the same numbers give 1.7 x 10^16 Pa (its conclusion is unchanged). Pg = GM^2/R^4 is only an order-of-magnitude estimate. Flagged for review.

blocks.prompt: Using Pg about GM^2/R^4, explain why a star whose internal pressure is less than Pg contracts.
blocks.explanation: Gravity pulls inward with a pressure of about Pg; if the outward gas pressure is smaller, there is a net inward force, so the star shrinks. As it shrinks its gas is compressed and heats up, raising the pressure, until balance is restored or the core collapses.

items: Stars form from nebulae; a stable star balances gravity and pressure (dP/dr = -G Mr rho_r / r^2).
Fusion of H to He powers stars; red giant, then white dwarf (low mass) or supernova, neutron star or black hole (high mass).
Massive stars live shortest; red dwarfs longest.
The Sun: 4.6 billion years old, on the main sequence.
